title: ExxonMobil (XOM) Stock Price Prediction: Bears still control the tape as XOM trades below key moving averages - Blockchain News
content: ExxonMobil (XOM) is trading at $161.78, below its 7-, 20- and 50-day moving averages, while momentum remains soft and Binance perpetual futures show aggressive selling pressure. Sanford C. Bernstei... ExxonMobil (XOM) closed the latest reading at $161.78, down 2.67% on the day and sitting near the lower half of its short-term range at $166.73 to $157.74. The stock is below its SMA 7 of $167.44, SMA 20 of $170.28 and SMA 50 of $173.17, which leaves the trend structure tilted lower for now. That matters because price is still trading under the moving-average stack, so rallies into overhead resistance are more likely to be sold unless the tape improves decisively. At the same time, the volume backdrop is not a panic flush. The reported volume regime is 0.47x versus the 5-day average, which points to a low-volume pullback rather than a disorderly liquidation. That usually means sellers are in control, but the move has not yet shown the kind of aggressive volume expansion that often accompanies a deeper break. The daily RSI sits at 34.73, which is still in the neutral zone but close to oversold territory. MACD is negative at -2.7254, and the histogram is flat at 0.0000, which tells you momentum is weak but not accelerating sharply right this second. Stochastic readings are also subdued, with %K at 25.70 and %D at 20.56, reinforcing the view that XOM is under pressure without yet showing a clean reversal trigger. Bollinger positioning is more useful here than the raw oscillator readings. XOM’s %B is 0.1988, putting the stock close to the lower band at $156.17. That makes the $156 area important: if it holds, the market can keep treating this as a stretched pullback; if it gives way, the chart opens into a more obvious downside break. The market has clearly drawn a short list of levels. Immediate support is $157.44, strong support is $153.09, immediate resistance is $166.43, and strong resistance is $171.07. The pivot point sits at $162.08, essentially right on top of the current price, which helps explain why XOM is hanging around an inflection zone rather than trending cleanly. On November 12, 2026, Bob Brackett at Sanford C. Bernstein lowered ExxonMobil’s price target to $186 from $193 while maintaining an Outperform rating. That is still above the current share price, but the cut itself is a reminder that expectations have moved lower. The target does not give XOM a near-term floor, but it does show that at least one named analyst still sees upside from current levels even after trimming the valuation view. There is no supplied earnings date, so the next catalyst timing is unknown from this evidence. That leaves the market focused on price behavior, not a scheduled event. Binance perpetual futures show a negative funding rate of -0.0721% on the 8-hour settlement, meaning shorts are paying longs. That can happen when bearish positioning is crowded or when the market is willing to pay to stay short, but funding alone does not prove conviction. Open interest is 3,441.55 contracts, with daily open interest value at $628,091 and a 24-hour change of 0.42%, so positioning is active but not exploding. The cleaner intraday signal is the taker flow. The taker buy/sell ratio is 0.6591, with buy volume of 434 versus sell volume of 658, which points to aggressive selling pressure. That fits the weak spot in the chart better than the slightly long-leaning account ratios. The account splits are only mildly bullish on paper: Binance global accounts are 51.2% long versus 48.8% short, and top-trader accounts are 54.0% long versus 46.0% short. Those ratios show a modest long bias in Binance cohorts, but they do not override the negative funding and stronger selling pressure in taker flow. XOM needs to reclaim the $166.43 to $171.07 resistance band to argue that the current pullback is stabilizing. Failure to hold $157.44 would leave $153.09 as the next key test, and a break there would shift the structure from a controlled pullback toward a more serious downside extension. The Texas-based integrated energy and chemical company, a constituent of the NYSE Composite, recently saw a research firm lower its rating from a top-tier bullish stance to neutral. The move came even as the company delivered a quarter that beat expectations, launched new oil production in Guyana and advanced a major gas project in Mozambique. With the shares pulling back sharply in a recent session, the market is now weighing strong fundamentals against signs that momentum may be cooling. A research firm recently cut ExxonMobil from its most bullish rating to a neutral stance, signaling a more cautious near-term view on the stock. Downgrades of this kind often reflect changes in earnings estimate trends or valuation rather than a negative view of the underlying business. The timing stands out, since the shares had already climbed substantially from their annual low. The downgrade suggests that much of the recent good news may already be reflected in the share price. Still, a single rating change rarely defines a stocks long-term direction, especially for a company with ExxonMobils scale, diversified operations and steady cash generation. ExxonMobils latest quarterly results were strong. The company posted  earnings per share that topped consensus estimates and improved dramatically from the same period a year earlier. Revenue also came in well ahead of expectations, reflecting solid production volumes and favorable conditions across parts of its business. Refining operations reportedly delivered particularly robust results, helping lift overall earnings. The companys net margin remains healthy, and return on equity is solid for an energy major. Market forecasts call for strong earnings across the full fiscal year, reinforcing the view that ExxonMobils diversified operations continue to generate substantial cash flow. ExxonMobil continues to expand its production base through major projects. The company recently started oil production at its Uaru project in Guyanas Stabroek block, a development that further boosts the countrys installed production capacity and strengthens ExxonMobils growth outlook. Guyana has become a cornerstone of the companys upstream strategy, offering high-quality, low-cost barrels. Meanwhile, Mozambique approved a plan connected to ExxonMobils Rovuma liquefied natural gas project, a step that could help move the large-scale gas development forward. Together, these projects highlight the companys ability to grow output across oil and natural gas, supporting long-term earnings visibility. ExxonMobils dividend remains a central part of its appeal. The companys latest dividend increase drew attention as a rare achievement, extending a long streak of annual payout growth that very few members of the  S&P 500 index can match. That consistency reinforces ExxonMobils reputation among income-focused market participants. Its  dividend yield offers a steady income stream, supported by the companys strong cash flow and conservative balance sheet. For a business exposed to volatile commodity prices, maintaining and growing the dividend through multiple energy cycles signals confidence in the durability of its earnings and financial discipline. ExxonMobil is an integrated energy and chemical company with operations spanning the entire oil and natural gas value chain. Its upstream business explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas, while its downstream operations refine and market fuels such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. The company also manufactures lubricants, petrochemical feedstocks and specialty materials used across consumer and industrial applications. Beyond traditional energy, ExxonMobil pursues lower-emission solutions, including carbon capture and storage, hydrogen and lower-emission fuels. This integrated model helps balance results across cycles, since weakness in production can be offset by strength in refining or chemicals. ExxonMobil belongs to the energy sector, where share prices often move in step with crude oil and natural gas prices. When commodity prices rise, producers typically see stronger cash flow, and when prices soften, margins can tighten. Refining conditions, global demand trends and production decisions by major oil-exporting nations also influence results. ExxonMobils integrated model and scale give it advantages over smaller producers, allowing it to weather downturns and fund long-term projects. The energy transition remains a key long-term theme, and the companys investments in carbon capture and hydrogen aim to position it for a lower-emission future. Sentiment among research firms covering ExxonMobil is mixed, with neutral ratings forming the largest group and favorable ratings close behind. A small number of firms take a bearish view. Over recent months, several firms raised their price targets, including a notable move to a high target with a favorable rating. Others trimmed targets while keeping bullish stances, and a new firm launched coverage with a neutral view. Overall, the average price target sits modestly above where the shares currently trade. That suggests market experts see some room for upside, though not as much as earlier in the year after the stocks strong run. ExxonMobil boasts one of the strongest balance sheets in the energy sector. Its debt-to-equity ratio is very low, reflecting minimal reliance on borrowed funds for a company of its size. The current ratio sits above parity, while the quick ratio is just below it, indicating solid liquidity. That financial strength allows the company to fund major projects, support its dividend and weather commodity downturns. The price-to-earnings ratio appears moderate, and the PEG ratio below parity suggests the valuation looks reasonable relative to expected growth. ExxonMobils beta sits far below the market average, meaning the stock has historically moved much less sharply than the broader market. Several factors will shape ExxonMobils path from here. Oil and natural gas prices remain the biggest drivers of earnings and sentiment. Production growth from Guyana will be closely watched, given its importance to the companys long-term strategy. Progress on the Rovuma LNG project in Mozambique could add a major new source of gas output over time. Refining margins will also matter, since they contributed meaningfully to recent results. Whether the stock can reclaim its intermediate moving average will be a key technical test. title: Is Exxon Mobil Stock a Good Fit For Your Portfolio Risk? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? If you own Exxon Mobil (XOM) or are about to, you likely hold it alongside money that already follows the S&P 500. Exxon is also a big bet on fuel. Management calls it the largest nonstate-owned refiner in the world. A stock like this can change how your whole portfolio behaves on the market’s good and bad days. How much depends on how much of it you hold. So does Exxon add to the market risk you already carry, or does it steady it? In the year to November 17, 2026, Exxon Mobil stock tended to move against the S&P 500. On the average day when the index rose 0.67%, a $10,000 holding in Exxon lost about $33. On the average day when the index fell 0.63%, that holding gained about $66. Exxon therefore steadied a market portfolio rather than adding to its risk. The stock recorded a beta of minus 0.56. Beta measures how far the stock moves when the index moves. A negative beta means the shares moved the other way on average. You received this offset alongside wider swings in Exxon itself. Its volatility, how widely its daily moves spread over a year, stood at 27.1%, compared with 13.8% for the index. Exxon did not offset every bad day. On November 5, 2026, the index’s worst day of that year, Exxon fell 2.3% while the S&P 500 fell 4.4%. Over the five years since November 9, 2021, Exxon returned 24.6% a year including dividends. The S&P 500 returned 10.9% a year. Exxon’s annual volatility over those five years sat at 26.7%, against 17.2% for the index. Dividing the return by the volatility reveals how much return each unit of swing earned. Exxon generated 0.92, against 0.63 for the S&P 500. The stock swung more than the market, but it paid you better for each swing. On its October 30, 2026 earnings call, management said Middle East conflict had constrained supplies of crude, diesel and gasoline. Management said this lack of supply led to higher market prices. An analyst asked when refining margins would return to normal. Management said it had no line of sight on how the many variables would play out. It guessed it would take well through 2027, possibly longer. Exxon’s results are tied to fuel markets that management itself cannot call. That uncertainty could keep the stock’s swings wide. The direction of those swings is less settled. Over the five years, Exxon’s daily moves had a weak positive correlation of 0.24 with the index. So moving against the market has not been its usual pattern. Exxon is expected to report in January 2027. The earnings of its Energy Products business are the number to watch. If the past year’s pattern holds, Exxon may trim your portfolio’s gain a little on the next day the market rises, and offset part of the loss on the next day it falls. If you already own other oil producers or refiners, though, you may hold a similar bet on fuel prices more than once, and their swings may add up rather than cancel. Exxon’s 24.6% a year came with a dividend that now yields 2.5%, a reminder that you do not have to pick between growth and income. Most portfolios settle for one. Chevron also turned 14.6% of its sales into operating profit, beating Exxon’s 12.4%. You therefore pay more for each dollar of Exxon’s profit, while Chevron grew faster and kept more of each sales dollar. Every other company in the group costs less per dollar of profit than Exxon. Only ConocoPhillips grew more slowly, at 13.3%, and its stock trades at a cheaper 14.5 times earnings. Because the oil producers and the refiners run different businesses from Exxon, their margins say less about it than Chevron’s margins do. You get one of the world’s biggest fuel businesses. Exxon’s Energy Products segment brought in $290 billion of its $324 billion revenue in fiscal 2025. That segment figure can include sales between Exxon’s own businesses. Management calls Exxon the largest nonstate-owned refiner in the world, running about 3.6 million barrels of crude a day through its refineries. Exxon’s total sales had an uneven year. Exxon’s revenue grew 2.6% from a year earlier in fiscal Q1 2026 and 32.6% in fiscal Q3 2026. The third quarter was also when, management said, conflict in the Middle East constrained supplies of crude, diesel and gasoline, and the lack of supply led to higher market prices. Buyers may be paying extra for something steadier: a long record of rewarding shareholders. On October 30, 2026, management announced a 4% dividend increase, marking its 44th consecutive year of dividend growth. Management plans to keep share repurchases at $20 billion in 2027, assuming reasonable market conditions. The company has also cut $16.9 billion of structural costs since 2019, toward a goal of $20 billion by 2030. The buyback plan was set while fuel was in short supply, and management said on the same call that it expects markets to take well through 2027 to get back closer to normal, possibly longer. So the price appears to assume Exxon can keep its profit and its payouts up once fuel markets settle. Its dividend record shows it has kept raising payouts through earlier downturns, but the four quarters behind today’s price end with a quarter of short supply, so they cannot show that yet. Exxon’s operating margin is the measure to watch in its fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027. Even the largest company in a group can trail its rivals for a year. That reality remains a good reason to spread your money across many strong businesses rather than lean on just one.  announced in November that it is advancing the next phase of its development offshore Guyana with Longtail, after the government of Guyana approved the Longtail Field Development Plan. The company said it has made a final investment decision on the project following the required government and regulatory approvals, with start-up targeted later this decade. The announcement keeps the company in focus for readers tracking Oil and Gas Stocks. Longtail will be another development in the Stabroek block and is located in the southeastern portion of the block. ExxonMobil is a constituent of the S&P 500, the NYSE Composite and the Russell 1000. It will develop non-associated gas and condensate-rich reservoirs, which ExxonMobil describes as marking a new phase for Stabroek. The company plans an additional investment of billions of dollars for the project. The Longtail FPSO is the central element of the development plan described in ExxonMobil's release. Its design capacity of more than a billion standard cubic feet per day of gas processing and thousands of barrels per day of condensate production reflects the nature of the reservoirs being developed, which contain non-associated gas and condensate rather than the oil-focused accumulations of earlier Stabroek projects. The planned billions of dollars investment is described in the release as an additional commitment for Longtail. ExxonMobil's statement ties the timing of first production later this decade, following construction of the FPSO and the drilling and completion of the subsea well network. The earlier Stabroek developments were built primarily to produce crude oil, with natural gas produced alongside the oil as associated gas. Longtail differs because its reservoirs hold non-associated gas, meaning gas that is found in reservoirs without a significant oil column, together with condensate-rich liquids. ExxonMobil's description of Longtail as marking a new phase for Stabroek reflects this shift in resource type. While the block's first several developments have centered on oil, Longtail introduces a development concept built around gas and condensate within the same block and partnership structure. ExxonMobil Guyana Limited is the operator of the Stabroek block and holds an interest. Hess Guyana Exploration Ltd. holds, and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana Limited holds the remaining, according to the release. Because the partners hold fixed percentage interests in the block, the planned investment and the resulting production from Longtail would be shared among ExxonMobil, Hess Guyana Exploration and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana in line with their respective stakes. According to the November release, production from the Stabroek block is thousands of barrels of oil per day from several projects. Another project, Uaru, is expected to start up in the fourth quarter, which ExxonMobil said would lift production above more than a million barrels per day. ExxonMobil's third-quarter results release, published in October noted that Guyana reached a cumulative milestone of more than a billion barrels. The same release cited volume growth in Guyana, alongside the Permian Basin and Golden Pass LNG, as a support for the company's year-to-date upstream earnings. Since earlier, ExxonMobil Guyana and its contractors have spent billions of dollars with Guyanese suppliers, according to the release. As additional projects such as Uaru, Whiptail, Hammerhead and Longtail move through construction and into operation, the company's Guyana disclosures will provide further updates on employment and local procurement. Longtail comes a few weeks after ExxonMobil reported its third-quarter results. The company recorded billions of dollars of earnings, or, compared with billions of dollars, or, in the second quarter. ExxonMobil declared a fourth-quarter dividend, payable in December to shareholders of record in November. The company has raised its annual dividend per share for dozens of consecutive years, a record it says is longer than that of nearly all S&P 500 companies. These moves add to a portfolio in which LNG projects sit alongside the oil-weighted Guyana and Permian assets. The third-quarter release identified Golden Pass LNG, alongside Guyana and the Permian Basin, as one of the sources of volume growth supporting year-to-date upstream earnings. Together with the planned interest increases in Papua LNG and Rovuma LNG, this places natural gas and LNG in a more prominent position within the company's upstream portfolio, a context in which the gas-focused Longtail development fits.
